title: The Quantum Revolution
description: Why classical physics broke down and how the quantum world was discovered

concepts.title: The Ultraviolet Catastrophe and Planck's Quantum
concepts.contentHtml:
Classical physics predicted a heated object should emit infinite power at ultraviolet frequencies — the 'ultraviolet catastrophe'. Every experiment showed this was wrong.

Max Planck (1900) solved the problem by assuming light energy comes in discrete chunks: E = hf, where h = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s (Planck's constant). This quantisation of energy tamed the infinity.

Planck thought it was a mathematical trick. Einstein took it seriously and used it to explain the photoelectric effect (1905), winning the Nobel Prize: light really is made of particles (photons), each with energy E = hf.

concepts.title: Wave-Particle Duality
concepts.contentHtml:
Light shows wave behaviour (interference, diffraction) and particle behaviour (photoelectric effect, Compton scattering). de Broglie (1924) proposed that matter also has a wavelength: λ = h/p, where p is momentum.

Davisson and Germer confirmed this in 1927 by diffracting electrons off a nickel crystal — electrons interfering like waves. A single electron fired at a double slit produces an interference pattern — but when you try to detect which slit it went through, the pattern vanishes.

The act of observation affects the system. This is not about clumsy measurement tools — it is fundamental to quantum mechanics.

concepts.title: Bohr's Atom and Energy Levels
concepts.contentHtml:
Rutherford's 1911 experiment showed atoms have a tiny dense nucleus with electrons orbiting it. But classical physics said orbiting electrons should radiate, lose energy, and spiral in — atoms should collapse in ~10⁻¹⁰ s.

Bohr (1913) proposed electrons can only occupy certain allowed orbits with quantised angular momentum. When an electron jumps between levels it emits or absorbs a photon with exactly the energy difference: ΔE = hf.

This explained hydrogen's spectral lines precisely. Though the full quantum mechanics came later, Bohr's model captured the key insight: atoms are stable because energy is quantised.

title: Wavefunctions and the Schrödinger Equation
description: The mathematical heart of quantum mechanics — probability waves and their evolution

concepts.title: The Wavefunction
concepts.contentHtml:
In quantum mechanics, a particle is described by a wavefunction ψ(x, t) — a complex-valued function. The wavefunction encodes all information about the particle.

The probability of finding the particle in a small region dx is |ψ|² dx. The wavefunction itself is not directly observable — only |ψ|² (the probability density) is physical.

The wavefunction must be normalised: the total probability of finding the particle somewhere is 1. This constraint ∫|ψ|² dx = 1 is a fundamental requirement.

concepts.title: The Schrödinger Equation
concepts.contentHtml:
Schrödinger (1926) wrote the equation governing how wavefunctions evolve in time:

iℏ ∂ψ/∂t = Ĥψ

where Ĥ is the Hamiltonian operator (total energy operator) and ℏ = h/2π.

For a particle in a potential V: Ĥ = −(ℏ²/2m)∇² + V. The time-independent version Ĥψ = Eψ gives the allowed energy levels (eigenvalues) and spatial wavefunctions (eigenstates) of the system.

Solving this equation for the hydrogen atom gives the exact same spectral lines Bohr had only approximated — a triumph of the new mechanics.

concepts.title: Heisenberg's Uncertainty Principle
concepts.contentHtml:
Heisenberg (1927) proved that position and momentum cannot both be known precisely simultaneously:

Δx · Δp ≥ ℏ/2

This is not a statement about imperfect measurement tools. It is fundamental: a particle with a well-defined position is in a superposition of many momenta, and vice versa.

Similarly, energy and time are an uncertainty pair: ΔE · Δt ≥ ℏ/2. This allows virtual particles to briefly violate energy conservation for a time Δt ~ ℏ/ΔE — the mechanism behind the Casimir effect and virtual processes in QED.

title: Superposition, Measurement, and Spin
description: Quantum states before and after observation — and the mystery of collapse

concepts.title: Superposition
concepts.contentHtml:
Quantum systems can exist in superpositions of multiple states simultaneously. Schrödinger's cat is a famous illustration: a cat in a box with a quantum trigger can be, before observation, in a superposition of alive and dead states.

Mathematically: if |0⟩ and |1⟩ are two basis states, |ψ⟩ = α|0⟩ + β|1⟩ with |α|² + |β|² = 1 is a valid superposition. Upon measurement, the result is |0⟩ with probability |α|² or |1⟩ with probability |β|².

This is not ignorance — the particle genuinely has no definite value before measurement. The experimental violation of Bell inequalities confirms this.

concepts.title: Measurement and Wavefunction Collapse
concepts.contentHtml:
Before measurement, a quantum system evolves smoothly via the Schrödinger equation. At the moment of measurement, the wavefunction appears to 'collapse' to a definite eigenstate — this is the measurement problem.

Different interpretations disagree on what 'collapse' means: Copenhagen says it's just an update of our knowledge. Many-Worlds says all outcomes happen, in branching universes. Pilot wave theory says there are hidden variables guiding a definite particle.

No experiment can currently distinguish between interpretations. The disagreement is philosophical, but the predictions of quantum mechanics are unambiguous — and universally confirmed.

concepts.title: Spin — An Intrinsic Quantum Property
concepts.contentHtml:
Electrons have an intrinsic angular momentum called spin — it has no classical analog. Spin-½ particles (electrons, protons, quarks) can be spin-up (+ℏ/2) or spin-down (−ℏ/2) along any axis.

The Stern-Gerlach experiment (1922) sent silver atoms through an inhomogeneous magnetic field and found only two spots on the detector — not a continuous spread. This was the first evidence of quantised spin.

Spin is the basis of MRI machines (nuclear spin), transistors (electron spin), and quantum computing (spin qubits). It's also responsible for the Pauli exclusion principle — no two fermions can occupy the same quantum state.

title: Entanglement and Non-Locality
description: Quantum correlations that 'spooky action at a distance' cannot explain classically

concepts.title: Quantum Entanglement
concepts.contentHtml:
Two particles can be prepared in an entangled state — their quantum states are correlated in a way that cannot be described by separate individual states.

The Bell state |Φ⁺⟩ = (|00⟩ + |11⟩)/√2 means: if Alice measures her particle and gets 0, Bob's particle is instantly 0 too, regardless of distance. Measuring up, Bob is also up.

Einstein called this 'spooky action at a distance' and believed it proved quantum mechanics was incomplete — there must be hidden local variables explaining the correlations. Bell's theorem and subsequent experiments proved Einstein wrong.

concepts.title: Bell's Theorem and Experiments
concepts.contentHtml:
John Bell (1964) proved that any local hidden variable theory predicts correlations satisfying the Bell inequality: |E(a,b) − E(a,c)| ≤ 1 + E(b,c). Quantum mechanics predicts violations of this inequality.

Alain Aspect's experiments (1982) definitively showed Bell inequality violations — quantum correlations are stronger than any classical local model allows. Loophole-free experiments in 2015 (Delft, NIST) confirmed this beyond all doubt.

Crucially, entanglement cannot be used to send information faster than light — the correlations are only apparent when the results are compared, which requires classical communication.

concepts.title: Quantum Teleportation and Cryptography
concepts.contentHtml:
Quantum teleportation (Bennett et al. 1993) uses an entangled pair to transfer a quantum state from Alice to Bob. The qubit state is destroyed at Alice's end and reconstructed at Bob's — matter teleportation science fiction remains fiction, but quantum state transmission is real.

Quantum key distribution (BB84 protocol) allows two parties to share a cryptographic key where any eavesdropping is detectable — measuring a quantum state disturbs it. This follows directly from the no-cloning theorem (unknown quantum states cannot be copied) and the measurement postulate.

title: Quantum Computing and Open Questions
description: Harnessing quantum mechanics — and the deep puzzles that remain

concepts.title: Qubits and Quantum Gates
concepts.contentHtml:
A classical bit is 0 or 1. A qubit is |ψ⟩ = α|0⟩ + β|1⟩ — a superposition. An n-qubit register can represent 2ⁿ states simultaneously.

Quantum gates manipulate qubits through unitary transformations. The Hadamard gate H puts a qubit into equal superposition: H|0⟩ = (|0⟩ + |1⟩)/√2. The CNOT gate entangles two qubits.

Quantum algorithms exploit superposition and interference to find answers faster. Shor's algorithm factors large numbers exponentially faster than classical algorithms — threatening RSA encryption. Grover's algorithm searches unsorted databases in √N steps instead of N.

concepts.title: Quantum Decoherence
concepts.contentHtml:
The main challenge in quantum computing is decoherence: quantum systems inevitably interact with their environment, causing superpositions to collapse and quantum information to be lost.

Decoherence explains why everyday objects don't exhibit quantum behaviour — they interact with ~10²³ particles constantly, instantly collapsing any superposition. Quantum computers must be isolated at millikelvin temperatures and shielded from vibration.

Decoherence also offers a partial answer to the measurement problem: the environment effectively measures the system, selecting one classical outcome from the quantum superposition. This is the 'many-worlds' picture — the superposition doesn't collapse; it entangles with the environment.

concepts.title: Quantum Gravity and Unresolved Questions
concepts.contentHtml:
Quantum mechanics governs the very small; general relativity governs the very large. Both are spectacularly confirmed — but they are mathematically incompatible. Unifying them is the central unsolved problem in theoretical physics.

Near singularities (black holes, Big Bang), both quantum effects and strong gravity matter simultaneously — and we have no theory. String theory and loop quantum gravity are leading candidates, but neither has unambiguous experimental confirmation.

Other open questions: Why is the quantum world probabilistic? Is the wavefunction real or epistemic? What is dark matter and dark energy — do they have a quantum description? The quantum revolution is still unfinished.

concepts.title: Penetrating a Barrier
concepts.contentHtml:
Classically, a particle without enough energy to surmount a potential barrier simply bounces off. Quantum mechanically, the wavefunction has a non-zero amplitude inside the barrier — and on the far side.

Tunneling probability falls exponentially with barrier width and √(barrier height − energy). Light barriers and thin barriers are easy; heavy particles or thick barriers see vanishing transmission.

For an electron at 1 eV through a 1 nm, 5 eV barrier, transmission is about 10⁻⁹ — small but nonzero. For a baseball, transmission is e^(-10⁴⁰), so don't hold your breath.

concepts.title: Alpha Decay & Stellar Fusion
concepts.contentHtml:
Why does an alpha particle escape a nucleus? Classically it shouldn't — the strong nuclear potential is far higher than its kinetic energy. Tunneling makes it possible.

Gamow's 1928 calculation used quantum tunneling to predict alpha decay rates accurately, validating QM in nuclear physics. Lifetimes span 60 orders of magnitude depending on the exponential tunneling factor.

Same physics governs stellar fusion: protons must tunnel through the Coulomb barrier. The Sun fuses very slowly because tunneling is rare; that slow rate is one reason main-sequence stars live 10 billion years.

concepts.title: Tunnel Diodes & STM
concepts.contentHtml:
Tunnel diodes exploit electron tunneling for ultra-fast switching. Scanning tunneling microscopes bring a sharp tip near a surface; tunneling current is exponentially sensitive to gap distance, allowing single-atom imaging.

Binnig and Rohrer won the 1986 Nobel for STM. Today's surface science can place individual atoms one at a time with these instruments.

Tunneling also matters in flash memory (electrons tunnel onto floating gates), Josephson junctions (Cooper-pair tunneling — basis of qubits), and increasingly in modern transistors as gate insulators shrink to nanometer thickness.

concepts.title: Sum Over All Paths
concepts.contentHtml:
In Feynman's formulation, the amplitude for a particle to go from A to B is a sum over all possible paths connecting them — straight, curved, even backward in time.

Each path contributes a complex amplitude e^(iS/ℏ), where S is the classical action of that path. Most paths cancel each other out by destructive interference. The classical trajectory survives because it's an extremum of S — neighboring paths share its phase and add up coherently.

Same physics, different lens. Path integrals make symmetries and quantum field theory beautifully natural.

concepts.title: Classical Limit
concepts.contentHtml:
For macroscopic objects, S ≫ ℏ. Tiny path differences mean huge phase differences — wild oscillations cancel everything except near the classical extremum.

This recovers Newtonian mechanics in the limit ℏ → 0. The classical trajectory is the one that extremizes the action, exactly as Lagrangian mechanics says.

The path integral makes the link clear: classical mechanics is the place where quantum interference is overwhelmingly biased toward one path.

concepts.title: Path Integrals in Field Theory
concepts.contentHtml:
Generalize from particles to fields and you have quantum field theory via path integrals. Sum over all field configurations weighted by e^(iS/ℏ) — that's how QED, QCD, and the Standard Model are formulated mathematically.

Wick rotation (t → -iτ) turns the oscillating phase into a real exponential — connecting QFT to statistical mechanics. This is why so much of modern theoretical physics shares techniques with condensed matter.

Path integrals also underpin lattice QCD, where field configurations are sampled numerically — the most successful first-principles calculation of hadron masses.

concepts.title: Copenhagen Interpretation
concepts.contentHtml:
The original (Bohr, Heisenberg, ~1925-1930): the wavefunction encodes possibilities; measurement causes collapse to a definite outcome; probabilities given by |ψ|².

It's pragmatic and predicts everything we measure. But what is 'measurement'? When does collapse happen? The Copenhagen view says these questions are unanswerable or unimportant — physics describes what we can predict and observe.

This was the orthodox view for decades, and it works in practice. Foundationalists find it incomplete.

concepts.title: Many-Worlds & Decoherence
concepts.contentHtml:
Everett (1957): there is no collapse. The universal wavefunction simply evolves according to Schrödinger's equation forever. What looks like collapse is the splitting of the world into branches — each containing a different measurement outcome.

Decoherence explains the appearance of classicality without invoking collapse: interaction with the environment makes branches effectively independent, with their interferences washed out.

Many-worlds is mathematically simple (no collapse postulate) but ontologically dramatic (uncountable parallel realities). Increasingly popular among working physicists, especially cosmologists.

concepts.title: Other Interpretations
concepts.contentHtml:
Pilot wave / Bohmian: particles have definite positions guided by a real wavefunction. Predicts the same statistics as Copenhagen but is deterministic.

QBism / relational: probabilities are subjective beliefs of an agent; measurement updates them. No external 'reality' for the wavefunction.

Objective collapse (GRW, Penrose): real spontaneous collapse, possibly triggered by gravity. Makes specific predictions (testable!) different from standard QM.

All current interpretations agree on every experimental prediction so far. The choice is partly philosophical — but new tabletop experiments may distinguish them in the next decade.
